lessons.title: RBI Rate Cycles, Inflation, and What They Do to Each Group

body.text: Interest rates reach your portfolio through two separate doors. The demand door decides how many cars and homes people buy, which drives cyclical earnings. The valuation door decides what multiple the market pays for future profits, which hits expensive defensives hardest. Inflation is a third axis entirely: it lifts commodity producers and squeezes commodity users.

children.text: Most investors know that rate cuts are good for stocks and rate hikes are bad. That is too blunt to be useful. A rate cut that revives car loans does almost nothing for a steel company whose prices are set in global markets. A rise in bond yields can knock 20% off a quality staples stock whose earnings never wobble. This lesson separates the channels, maps them to the five positions on the spectrum, and walks through India's actual rate and inflation cycle.

When the RBI changes the repo rate, banks reprice loans that are linked to an external benchmark, usually within a quarter. EMIs on home and car loans move, and so does the cost of working capital and project finance for companies. Chapter 2 showed the arithmetic: a one percentage point change in a 20-year home loan rate moves the EMI by thousands of rupees a month and changes how much a buyer can borrow. This channel hits early cyclicals first, late cyclicals later through capex decisions, and barely touches a soap maker.

The second channel has nothing to do with sales. Every stock is priced off a required return, and that return is built on the risk-free rate, which in India is anchored by the 10-year government bond yield. When yields rise, required returns rise, and the present value of distant profits falls. Chapter 3 showed why this hurts high-P/E defensives most: a one point rise in the required return cut the illustrative StapleCo's justified P/E by about a quarter, roughly twice the hit to a cyclical trading at a single-digit multiple.

body.text: This is why a defensive label does not mean safe from rate hikes. In a tightening cycle, a staples leader at 60 times earnings can fall as much as a cyclical, but for a completely different reason: its profits are intact and its multiple is shrinking. Knowing which door the damage came through tells you whether to worry about the business or about the price you paid.

body.title: Repo Rate at Selected RBI Policy Decisions (%)

events.title: Emergency easing
events.description: The RBI cut the repo rate to 4%, its lowest in decades, to support an economy shut down by the pandemic. Cheap money helped fuel the recovery in autos, housing, and credit.

events.title: The tightening cycle
events.description: With inflation running well above the 6% upper tolerance limit, the RBI raised the repo rate in steps from 4% to 6.5%, starting with an off-cycle hike in May 2022.

events.title: The long pause
events.description: The repo rate stayed at 6.5% for about two years while inflation gradually came down.

events.title: Aggressive easing
events.description: With inflation collapsing, the RBI cut 125 basis points across the year: to 6.25% in February, 6% in April, a larger 50 basis point cut to 5.5% in June, and 5.25% in December. It also cut the cash reserve ratio by 100 basis points, from 4% to 3%, in four tranches.

events.title: On hold
events.description: As inflation normalised back towards 4%, the MPC held the repo rate at 5.25% with a neutral stance, including at its August 2026 meeting.

markDefs.definition: The framework under which the RBI targets consumer price inflation of 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. It was introduced in 2016 and the target was retained for April 2026 to March 2031.

children.text: Rates do not move at random. Under

, CPI inflation is what the RBI is chasing, so tracking inflation tells you where rates are likely to go next. India's recent swing was extraordinary: CPI inflation fell to 0.25% in October 2025, the lowest on record, helped by food prices falling about 5% year on year, and then climbed back to 4.45% by July 2026. That collapse is what made the 2025 rate cuts possible, and the normalisation since is why the RBI has been on hold.

children.text: Timing matters as much as direction. A commodity producer's realisation rises the moment global prices rise. A consumer company's costs rise immediately, but it can usually only raise prices with a lag of a quarter or two, and it risks losing volume if it moves too fast. That gap is why input cost spikes compress consumer margins first and repair them later, while the same spike inflates producer margins at once.

body.caption: A rough gauge of how restrictive policy is; the RBI looks at expected inflation, not just the latest print

body.title: How Restrictive Is Policy?
body.prompt: In July 2026, CPI inflation was 4.45% and the repo rate was 5.25%. What was the real policy rate, in percentage points? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 5.25% minus 4.45% = 0.80 percentage points. Compare that with October 2025, when inflation was 0.25% and the repo rate was 5.50%: the real rate was then above 5 percentage points, extremely restrictive, which is exactly why the RBI kept cutting. When inflation rises towards the repo rate, the room for further cuts shrinks.

body.title: Why bond yields matter more than the repo rate for valuations

children.text: The repo rate is an overnight rate. It anchors short-term borrowing costs and floating rate loans, so it drives the demand channel. Equity valuations discount profits many years into the future, so they key off long-term rates, which is why the 10-year government bond yield is the number to watch for the valuation channel.

The two do not always move together. Long yields also reflect government borrowing, global bond markets, and expectations about inflation years ahead. The RBI can cut the repo rate while the 10-year yield rises, if markets fear heavy borrowing or higher future inflation. When that happens, rate-sensitive cyclicals get their demand boost while high-multiple defensives get no valuation relief.

body.title: Which Door Did the Damage?
body.question: Bond yields rise sharply. A staples company trading at 60 times earnings falls 18%, while its volumes, margins, and profit guidance are all unchanged. What happened?
options: Its earnings must be about to collapse
The valuation channel: a higher required return compressed the multiple investors will pay for distant profits
The demand channel: higher EMIs reduced soap consumption
Nothing meaningful; high-P/E stocks are unaffected by interest rates
body.explanation: Everyday consumption barely responds to interest rates, so the demand channel is not the cause. The damage came through the valuation door: higher yields raise the required return, and the more of a company's value sits in distant future profits, the more its multiple falls.

body.title: The Cuts Have Started
body.scenario: Meena follows the RBI closely. Over one year, the repo rate falls from 6.5% to 5.5%, inflation is below 2%, and the RBI also cuts the cash reserve ratio to release liquidity into the banking system. She wants to reposition her portfolio, which is currently three quarters in FMCG and pharma funds. Her plan is to sell all of it and buy an infrastructure fund and two housing finance stocks.
body.prompt: What is sound in Meena's thinking, and what would you push back on?
body.modelAnswer: The direction is defensible. Falling rates and ample liquidity typically help early cyclicals first, and housing finance sits directly in that path, while infrastructure is a late cyclical that benefits only once capex actually picks up, so those two are not the same bet. What deserves pushback is the completeness and the timing. Selling all defensive exposure removes the part of the portfolio that protects her if growth disappoints or if the easing is happening because the economy is weak. Rate cuts also support defensive valuations through the valuation channel, so they are not automatically the wrong thing to own. And markets anticipate: by the time a year of cuts is visible, rate-sensitive stocks have often already rerated, so she should check what is priced in using the Chapter 4 tools. A measured tilt, adding early cyclicals while keeping a defensive core, and watching credit growth and vehicle sales to confirm demand is actually responding, is a better plan than switching the whole portfolio at once.

body.title: Anchor for Valuations
body.textWithBlank: Because equity valuations discount profits far into the future, the ___ year government bond yield matters more for the valuation channel than the overnight repo rate.
body.explanation: The 10-year government bond yield is India's benchmark long-term risk-free rate, so it anchors the required return investors apply to distant profits.

body.title: Track the Rate and Inflation Cycle
steps: Note the repo rate and the MPC stance after each policy meeting, and whether the vote was split
Track monthly CPI inflation against the 4% target and the 2% to 6% band
Separate food inflation from core inflation, since the RBI reacts differently to each
Calculate the real policy rate to judge how restrictive policy is
Watch the 10-year government bond yield for the valuation channel, not just the repo rate
Check whether rate changes are reaching borrowers, using bank credit growth and lending rate data
Map the stage of the cycle to your holdings: which are exposed through demand, which through valuation

points: Rates work through two channels: demand, which drives cyclical earnings, and valuation, which compresses or expands multiples
Early cyclicals feel the demand channel first; richly valued defensives feel the valuation channel hardest
Deep cyclicals respond more to global commodity prices than to RBI policy
Under flexible inflation targeting, CPI drives policy, so tracking inflation tells you where rates are heading
India's cycle ran from a 4% repo rate in 2020 to 6.5% by February 2023, then 125 basis points of cuts in 2025 to 5.25%, held through 2026
Commodity inflation helps producers immediately and squeezes users first, because consumer companies can only pass on costs with a lag
